headline: David Flanagan sees RBA holding rates with hawkish tone maintained well into cycle, market pricing near-zero probability of move
reasoning: Flanagan noted the RBA held rates unanimously and markets had virtually nothing priced in for a move at this meeting. He highlighted that the RBA's statement retains hawkish language — noting the board will increase rates further if upside risks materialise — and argued the RBA learned from the previous cycle where markets priced in overly low terminal rates too quickly. He expects the RBA to keep a hawkish tone in play for some time before releasing the handbrake. Inflation is forecast to remain above 3% until mid-2027 and return to the 2.5% band by early 2028.
quote: Seems a little softer on whether they need to hike or not. Obviously they've they've a unanimous decision to denote that, but says the board will continue to do what's necessary to bring inflation sustainably black, including increasing their cash rate further if upside risks materialize. So we're still got that hawkish ness there. I think they've learnt from the last cycle where, you know, the market got really, uh um keen on rate cuts. And we saw some pretty low terminal rates priced in. I think that the RBA is going to take some time before they are release the handbrake here. They're going to keep the hawkish tone well in play for some time.

headline: RBA holding rates but market still pricing better-than-even chance of a hike by year-end; global central bank pressure also relevant
reasoning: Flanagan observed that while nothing was priced in for the current meeting, markets were still pricing in a better-than-even chance of a rate lift by year-end. He flagged that global central banks, including the Fed, face pressure to lift rates, adding to the uncertainty around the Australian rate outlook.

Uh off the back of what we do hear from the RBA because pressure on a number of central banks around the world to to lift rates. Interestingly, of course, what the fed is likely to do that remains an open question.

headline: David Flanagan flags oil supply disruption through the Strait of Hormuz as a persistent upside inflation risk that could yet bite discretionary spending
reasoning: Flanagan notes that the disruption of global oil supply through the Strait of Hormuz has so far been offset by drawdowns of global reserves, but this cannot continue indefinitely. The RBA itself explicitly acknowledges oil prices as a risk in its statement. If fuel prices continue to rise, either consumers pull back elsewhere or reduce travel, creating a broader drag on discretionary spending. He views the situation as handled reasonably well so far but flags it as something to watch.
quote: We still don't know where oil prices are likely to go. Are they? Because no one is none the wiser as far as the outcome in the Middle East is concerned. They keep saying the bottleneck could be coming because obviously the impact of the oil, um, shortage, if you will, or the lack of oil coming through the Strait of Hormuz is being offset by drawdowns of, you know, global reserves. And at some point it has to bite yet to see whether that actually happens. So there is a bit of anxiousness. And you can see in the RBA's commentary they mention it around oil prices.

headline: David Flanagan sees Australian inflation remaining above 3% until mid-2027, with unemployment rising to 4.8% by end-2028 and activity slowing in H2
reasoning: Flanagan notes the RBA's updated forecasts show inflation staying above 3% until mid-2027 and not returning to the 2.5% midpoint until early 2028. Unemployment is forecast to reach 4.6% by mid-next year and 4.8% by end of the forecast period, up from prior estimates of 4.4%. He highlights a dual signal from banks: loan applications are slowing while deposit growth is rising rapidly, suggesting animal spirits are being dampened by both rate hikes and tax changes. This behavioural shift points to a likely slowdown in household spending and investment activity through the back half of the year, which could push inflation lower than currently anticipated. He flags oil supply disruption through the Strait of Hormuz as an additional upside risk to inflation that is being watched carefully.
quote: They've made some pretty big changes to headline inflation. Obviously is a lower starting point than previously expected. Trimmed mean has been lowered as well. Um, so the trajectory with lower starting point um, but it sticks around a little longer. Interestingly, growth's been upgraded. Uh, which is interesting concept given we're probably looking down the barrel of lower activity potentially in the back half this year. And then you look at they've lifted their unemployment forecast. So we're now looking at unemployment getting up towards 4.8% by December 28th. At the end of their forecast period. Um, and even getting as high as 4.6 by the middle of next year, up from 4.4 previously. So there's clearly some some headwinds there which should help inflation. I think inflation, you know, if we do see this stalling in credit growth and rising household deposits in the banking system, that activity could actually slow a little further than is anticipated at the moment.

headline: David Flanagan sees peak RBA rates as likely but oil prices remain the clear and present danger to the inflation outlook
reasoning: Flanagan believes it is likely Australia has seen peak rates but flags oil as the key residual risk. He notes the RBA's May SMP assumed Brent at just over $100/barrel, now revised down to $95, with an assumption of ~$80 by year-end settling in the mid-70s. He argues this is a rosy assumption and even a brief spike back to $100 could materially knock the inflation forecast. He views the RBA's hawkish tone as apt and sees no reason for the central bank to ease up at this stage.
quote: I think it's likely we have. And I think there's still going to be risks. I just had a bit of a comparison of the oil forecast that's been in the assumptions to the RBA's forecasts. And the only real difference between the SMP and Mae. And now is that in June, in the May statement, they were expecting it to be just over $100 a barrel for Brent, and it's now down to 95 in their assumptions. But going forward, they still see it going down to 80, but just over 80 bucks by the end of the year. And then sort of settling back in that mid 70 range. So I would say that the RBA's sentiment of being still solidly hawkish is probably apt. At the moment. I can't see any reason why they would want to take their foot completely off the throat.

headline: David Flanagan warns Australian housing shortages will persist and drive house prices materially higher again from next year as confidence returns
reasoning: Flanagan argues that the underlying structural shortage of housing in Australia remains unresolved. He expects that as confidence returns to the market, demand will re-emerge and push house prices significantly higher, which he describes as unfortunate for prospective first-home buyers. The near-term dampening effect of rate hikes and tax changes on loan applications and borrowing is temporary in his view.
quote: everyone will realize that those those underlying shortages of housing that we're still dealing with are still there and confidence will return. And unfortunately, that will that will start pushing house prices much, uh, much higher again, unfortunately for those who are who are trying to get into the housing market next year.
